metadata.original_text: This time series records neodymium CNY T data in the Commodity market price domain, with a collection frequency of daily, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2023-06-23 to 2023-07-10. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On May 16, 2023, Noveon Magnetics, a U.S.-based manufacturer of sustainable neodymium rare earth magnets, announced the closure of a $75 million Series B funding round. [6, 7] The round was led by NGP Energy Capital Management LLC and Aventurine Partners. [3, 4, 5, 6] The company intends to use the funds to accelerate the expansion of its 145,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in San Marcos, Texas. [3, 4, 5, 6] This expansion is aimed at increasing production to meet the significant global demand for rare earth magnets, which are critical components in the automotive, defense, energy, medical, and consumer goods sectors. [3, 4, 6] Noveon plans to ramp up production to approximately 2,000 tons of magnets annually by 2024. [3, 4, 5, 6] <2> On May 4, 2023, MP Materials announced its financial results for the first quarter ending March 31, 2023, reporting a 42% year-over-year decrease in revenue. This decline was driven by a 32% decrease in the realized price of rare earth oxide (REO) and a 13% decline in sales volumes. The company stated that the lower prices reflected a softer pricing environment for rare earth products compared to the peak prices observed in the same period of the previous year. <3> On February 16, 2023, Texas Governor Greg Abbott delivered his biennial State of the State address from the factory floor of Noveon Magnetics, a neodymium rare earth magnet manufacturer in San Marcos, Texas. [4, 8] Bucking the tradition of speaking before a joint legislative session at the Capitol, Abbott used the address to outline seven emergency items for the 88th legislative session, including property tax cuts, ending COVID-19 restrictions, and border security. [5, 9] During the speech, Abbott highlighted the company as a "cutting-edge business in the critical field of rare earth elements" and emphasized the need for U.S. self-reliance, stating, "The future of Texas and the United States should not depend on China." [3, 9] <4> On January 26, 2023, the Progressive Policy Institute released a policy paper titled 'Rare Earths for America's Future,' which details the United States' dependency on China for rare earth elements (REEs). [1, 2] The paper asserts that for the last 20 years, the U.S. has been almost entirely reliant on China for these 17 metallic elements, which are crucial for national security and economic prosperity. [1, 2] It provides a strategic framework to build a sustainable domestic REE industry, focusing on streamlined permitting, tax reforms, and high-impact research and development. [1] Key recommendations include introducing tax incentives for domestic REE producers, establishing a federal body to coordinate mine permitting, creating a federal REE recycling program, and prioritizing federal support for the development of REE alternatives. [1, 2] <5> MP Materials, owner of the only operational rare earth mine in the U.S., entered into a definitive supply agreement with General Motors to provide U.S.-sourced and manufactured rare earth materials, alloy, and finished magnets for GM's electric vehicle programs. [2, 10] The binding long-term agreement was first announced on December 9, 2021, with the definitive agreement announced on April 21, 2022. [5, 2] Production is expected to gradually ramp up starting in late 2023. [2, 10] Separately, on February 22, 2022, MP Materials was awarded a $35 million contract from the U.S. Department of Defense to support the construction of a facility to refine and separate heavy rare earth elements at its Mountain Pass, California site, advancing the goal of creating a complete domestic rare earth supply chain. [1, 3, 4, 6]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Ucore Rare Metals Inc. announced on July 13, 2023, that it had conducted an initial post-award conference with the US Department of Defense (DoD). [1] This meeting was a key step following a US$4 million agreement aimed at prototyping and developing domestic rare earth element (REE) separation capabilities. [1] The project's goal is to demonstrate and advance solutions for REE separation to strengthen the US and Canadian supply chain, reduce vulnerabilities, and support defense manufacturing sectors. [1] The conference outlined the planned schedule to utilize Ucore's RapidSX™ technology at its facility in Kingston, Ontario, with the ultimate aim of establishing a full-scale processing facility in North America. [1] <2> On July 3, 2023, China's Ministry of Commerce and General Administration of Customs announced new export licensing requirements for gallium and germanium, materials critical to the semiconductor, electronics, and other high-tech industries. The move, which became effective on August 1, 2023, requires exporters to obtain a license before shipping the specified metals and their chemical compounds. While the announcement did not single out any specific country, it was widely viewed in the United States as a retaliatory measure and an escalation in the ongoing trade dispute over technology, following export controls on semiconductors imposed by the U.S. and its allies. This action raised significant concerns about the stability of the global supply chain for these critical minerals, given China's dominant position as a producer. <3> On May 16, 2023, Noveon Magnetics, a U.S.-based manufacturer of sustainable neodymium rare earth magnets, announced the closure of a $75 million Series B funding round. [3, 4, 5, 6] The company intends to use the funds to accelerate the expansion of its 145,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in San Marcos, Texas. [3, 4, 5, 6] This expansion is aimed at increasing production to meet the significant global demand for rare earth magnets, which are critical components in the automotive, defense, energy, medical, and consumer goods sectors. [3, 4, 6] Noveon plans to ramp up production to approximately 2,000 tons of magnets annually by 2024. [4, 8] Bucking the tradition of speaking before a joint legislative session at the Capitol, Abbott used the address to outline seven emergency items for the 88th legislative session, including property tax cuts, ending COVID-19 restrictions, and border security. [5, 9] During the speech, Abbott highlighted the company as a "cutting-edge business in the critical field of rare earth elements" and emphasized the need for U.S. self-reliance, stating, "The future of Texas and the United States should not depend on China." [1, 2] The paper asserts that for the last 20 years, the U.S. has been almost entirely reliant on China for these 17 metallic elements, which are crucial for national security and economic prosperity. [1, 2] It provides a strategic framework to build a sustainable domestic REE industry, focusing on streamlined permitting, tax reforms, and high-impact research and development. [1] Key recommendations include introducing tax incentives for domestic REE producers, establishing a federal body to coordinate mine permitting, creating a federal REE recycling program, and prioritizing federal support for the development of REE alternatives. [1, 2] <7> MP Materials, owner of the only operational rare earth mine in the U.S., entered into a definitive supply agreement with General Motors to provide U.S.-sourced and manufactured rare earth materials, alloy, and finished magnets for GM's electric vehicle programs. [2, 10] The binding long-term agreement was first announced on December 9, 2021, with the definitive agreement announced on April 21, 2022. [5, 2] Production is expected to gradually ramp up starting in late 2023. [2, 10] Separately, on February 22, 2022, MP Materials was awarded a $35 million contract from the U.S. Department of Defense to support the construction of a facility to refine and separate heavy rare earth elements at its Mountain Pass, California site, advancing the goal of creating a complete domestic rare earth supply chain. [1, 3, 4, 6]

[4, 8] Bucking the tradition of speaking before a joint legislative session at the Capitol, Abbott used the address to outline seven emergency items for the 88th legislative session, including property tax cuts, ending COVID-19 restrictions, and border security. [5, 9] During the speech, Abbott highlighted the company as a "cutting-edge business in the critical field of rare earth elements" and emphasized the need for U.S. self-reliance, stating, "The future of Texas and the United States should not depend on China." Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> China's Northern Rare Earth Group announced on August 1, 2024, that its listed prices for rare earth products for that month would be unchanged from July 2024. The price for praseodymium-neodymium oxide was held at 384,800 yuan per ton. This decision by a major global supplier had a significant impact on market confidence at the beginning of the month. While prices were stable at the time of the announcement, by the end of August, praseodymium-neodymium oxide prices had increased by 7.5% compared to the beginning of the month. <2> On July 16, 2024, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced nearly $10 million in funding for two projects aimed at lowering the costs and reducing the environmental impact of producing rare earth elements and other critical minerals from coal and its by-products. The projects, awarded under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, will concentrate on advanced laboratory and bench-scale testing to improve the economic viability of separation and refining technologies. <3> On May 14, 2024, the U.S. Trade Representative, Katherine Tai, announced a significant shift in the nation's tariff policy regarding China following a statutory four-year review of the Section 301 tariffs. [3, 4, 8] This action is intended to protect American workers and businesses from what the administration deems China's unfair trade practices, including technology transfer-related policies and cyber theft. [4, 8, 9] The directive includes increasing tariffs on approximately $18 billion worth of imports in strategic sectors. [3, 9] Specifically, tariffs on certain critical minerals will increase to 25% in 2024, and tariffs on permanent magnets, crucial for electric vehicles and wind turbines, will rise to 25% in 2026. [2, 5, 11] This is the first time rare earth magnets have been included in the Section 301 tariffs. [2, 11] <4> MP Materials has been awarded a $58.5 million Section 48C Advanced Energy Project tax credit by the U.S. IRS and Treasury to support the construction of its rare earth magnet manufacturing facility in Fort Worth, Texas. Announced on April 1, 2024, the award advances a project that began construction in April 2022 and is a key part of America's strategy to build a domestic supply chain for critical materials. The facility will be the first of its kind in the U.S., designed for the end-to-end production of neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) magnets, which are vital for electric vehicles, wind turbines, and defense applications. Raw materials will be sourced from MP Materials' mine in Mountain Pass, California, and processed into finished magnets at the Fort Worth plant. The company expects to start commercial production of precursor materials in the summer of 2024 and finished magnets by late 2025, with General Motors as a foundational customer. <5> Cyclic Materials, a Canadian advanced metals recycling company, and VACUUMSCHMELZE (VAC), a German developer of magnetic materials, announced a partnership to create a circular supply chain for rare earth elements. [2, 4, 8] Under the agreement, by-products from VAC's manufacturing of high-performance neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) permanent magnets will be recycled using Cyclic Materials' proprietary processes in North America. [2, 3, 5] This collaboration aims to establish a sustainable, local supply chain for critical materials essential for electric vehicles, wind turbines, and modern electronics, reducing the need for new mining. [2, 6, 8] The recycled raw materials are expected to have a carbon footprint up to 75% lower than mined materials, enabling VAC's customers to source magnets with lower Scope 3 emissions. [2, 5] The partnership aligns with VAC's plans to construct a magnet manufacturing plant in the U.S. with support from the Department of Defense. [3] <6> The United States is actively working to integrate Central Asia into its critical mineral supply chains, a strategic effort to diversify sources for materials like neodymium and reduce reliance on single suppliers such as China. [1] This initiative was formally advanced with the inaugural meeting of the Critical Minerals Dialogue (CMD) in the C5+1 format—comprising the United States and the five Central Asian nations (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan)—which took place on February 8, 2024. [1, 2, 3, 4] The dialogue, hosted by the U.S. Department of State, aims to foster investment and cooperation in the region's significant mineral reserves, which include 38.6% of global manganese ore and 30.07% of chromium. [1] The CMD was first announced during the C5+1 Presidential Summit in New York on September 19, 2023. [3] The dialogue seeks to increase Central Asia's involvement in global supply chains, promote economic cooperation, and support the clean energy transition while adhering to high environmental, social, and governance standards. [3, 4] <7> On January 31, 2024, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) released its annual Mineral Commodity Summaries 2024 report. [2, 4] This document provides a comprehensive overview of global mineral trends and serves as the earliest source of 2023 mineral production data for the world. [2, 4] The report covers more than 90 individual nonfuel minerals and materials, including detailed statistics on rare earth elements like neodymium. [2, 6] It presents data on domestic industry structure, government programs, tariffs, and five-year salient statistics, along with world production and reserves. [4] The 2024 summary highlights that the value of U.S. nonfuel mineral production was an estimated $105 billion in 2023. [8] It also underscores the nation's continued reliance on foreign sources for numerous mineral commodities, being 100% import-dependent for 15 and over 50% reliant for another 49. [1] <8> The 'Critical Minerals Security Act of 2024' (S.3631) was introduced in the U.S. Senate on January 18, 2024. [6] The bipartisan legislation, sponsored by senators John Cornyn (R-TX) and Mark Warner (D-VA), aims to reduce U.S. reliance on foreign entities, particularly China, for critical minerals and rare earth elements essential for national security and technology. [6, 5] The bill directs the Secretary of the Interior to submit comprehensive reports to Congress on global critical mineral resources. [1, 8] These reports must assess which resources are controlled by the U.S. or its allies versus those controlled by foreign entities of concern. [1, 5] The act also mandates the formulation of a national strategy to develop advanced domestic technologies for mining, refining, separation, and processing of these key minerals. [1] <9> To protect its global market dominance in the rare earths sector, China's Ministry of Commerce officially banned the export of technology for the extraction and separation of these strategic metals on December 21, 2023. [2, 3, 9] The ban was an update to the country's "Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited and Restricted from Export" and also includes technology for producing rare earth metals, alloy materials, and certain magnets. [3, 6, 9] This policy move is seen as a measure to safeguard national security and maintain China's significant control over the industry, where it accounts for nearly 90% of global refined output. [6, 8] The decision has major implications for the United States and European nations, which are actively seeking to develop their own domestic supply chains for critical minerals, like neodymium, to reduce their dependence on Chinese processing. [3, 6] While China had discouraged the export of this technology for years, this official ban formalizes its position amidst escalating competition with the West over control of critical minerals. [4, 8]

Firstly, on December 21, 2023, the government officially banned the export of technology for extracting and separating rare earths. [7, 12, 11] This was followed by the announcement on June 29, 2024, of a broader set of regulations titled the 'Regulations on the Administration of Rare Earths', which became effective on October 1, 2024. [3, 4] Key measures include the implementation of a total quantity control system for mining and separation, and the establishment of a product traceability system. [3, 5] Given that China processes nearly 90% of the world's rare earths, these actions are anticipated to have a substantial impact on the global supply chain and have heightened concerns in countries like the United States, which rely heavily on Chinese rare earth imports. [3, 4, 8] This action is intended to protect American workers and businesses from what the administration deems China's unfair trade practices, including technology transfer-related policies and cyber theft. [4, 8, 9] The directive includes increasing tariffs on approximately $18 billion worth of imports in strategic sectors. [3, 9] Specifically, tariffs on certain critical minerals will increase to 25% in 2024, and tariffs on permanent magnets, crucial for electric vehicles and wind turbines, will rise to 25% in 2026. [2, 5, 11] This is the first time rare earth magnets have been included in the Section 301 tariffs. Announced on April 1, 2024, the award advances a project that began construction in April 2022 and is a key part of America's strategy to build a domestic supply chain for critical materials. The facility will be the first of its kind in the U.S., designed for the end-to-end production of neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) magnets, which are vital for electric vehicles, wind turbines, and defense applications. Raw materials will be sourced from MP Materials' mine in Mountain Pass, California, and processed into finished magnets at the Fort Worth plant. [2, 6, 8] The recycled raw materials are expected to have a carbon footprint up to 75% lower than mined materials, enabling VAC's customers to source magnets with lower Scope 3 emissions. [2, 5] The partnership aligns with VAC's plans to construct a magnet manufacturing plant in the U.S. with support from the Department of Defense. [1] This initiative was formally advanced with the inaugural meeting of the Critical Minerals Dialogue (CMD) in the C5+1 format—comprising the United States and the five Central Asian nations (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan)—which took place on February 8, 2024. [1, 2, 3, 4] The dialogue, hosted by the U.S. Department of State, aims to foster investment and cooperation in the region's significant mineral reserves, which include 38.6% of global manganese ore and 30.07% of chromium. [1] The CMD was first announced during the C5+1 Presidential Summit in New York on September 19, 2023. [3] The dialogue seeks to increase Central Asia's involvement in global supply chains, promote economic cooperation, and support the clean energy transition while adhering to high environmental, social, and governance standards. [3, 4] <8> On January 31, 2024, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) released its annual Mineral Commodity Summaries 2024 report. [2, 4] This document provides a comprehensive overview of global mineral trends and serves as the earliest source of 2023 mineral production data for the world. [2, 4] The report covers more than 90 individual nonfuel minerals and materials, including detailed statistics on rare earth elements like neodymium. [2, 6] It presents data on domestic industry structure, government programs, tariffs, and five-year salient statistics, along with world production and reserves. [4] The 2024 summary highlights that the value of U.S. nonfuel mineral production was an estimated $105 billion in 2023. [8] It also underscores the nation's continued reliance on foreign sources for numerous mineral commodities, being 100% import-dependent for 15 and over 50% reliant for another 49. [1] <9> The 'Critical Minerals Security Act of 2024' (S.3631) was introduced in the U.S. Senate on January 18, 2024. [6] The bipartisan legislation, sponsored by senators John Cornyn (R-TX) and Mark Warner (D-VA), aims to reduce U.S. reliance on foreign entities, particularly China, for critical minerals and rare earth elements essential for national security and technology. [6, 5] The bill directs the Secretary of the Interior to submit comprehensive reports to Congress on global critical mineral resources. [1, 8] These reports must assess which resources are controlled by the U.S. or its allies versus those controlled by foreign entities of concern. [1, 5] The act also mandates the formulation of a national strategy to develop advanced domestic technologies for mining, refining, separation, and processing of these key minerals. [1]

Prediction target period: from 2025-02-10 to 2025-02-25. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In a significant milestone for the American domestic supply chain, MP Materials announced it has commenced commercial production of neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) metal at its 'Independence' facility in Fort Worth, Texas. [2, 4, 6] The announcement also confirmed the start of trial production for automotive-grade neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) magnets. [2, 8] This development is a key step in re-establishing a fully integrated U.S. mine-to-magnet supply chain, with raw materials sourced from the company's Mountain Pass mine in California. [4, 8] The facility is expected to produce approximately 1,000 metric tons of finished magnets annually, with a significant portion allocated to customers like General Motors for use in electric vehicles. [2, 5, 8] <2> MP Materials announced it has commenced commercial production of neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) metal at its new 'Independence' manufacturing facility in Fort Worth, Texas. The company also began trial production of automotive-grade, sintered neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) magnets at the same site. This marks a significant milestone in the company's $700 million investment to restore a fully integrated domestic supply chain for rare earth magnets in the United States, which have been almost entirely imported for decades. The facility, which began construction in April 2022, will source its raw materials from MP Materials' mine in Mountain Pass, California, and is expected to produce approximately 1,000 metric tons of finished magnets annually. General Motors is a foundational customer for the magnets, which will be used in the electric motors for its EV programs. <3> The inauguration of President Donald Trump's new administration on January 20, 2025, created significant uncertainty in the U.S. rare earth market. [1, 2, 3] Market participants anticipated disruption due to the administration's trade policies, particularly proposed tariffs on Chinese goods which include critical rare earth materials. [13] Plans were indicated to impose broad tariffs, potentially including a 25% tariff on imports from Mexico and Canada and an additional 10% on goods from China, which observers noted could lead to higher domestic prices for rare earths in the long term. [13] A central theme of the administration's approach is to bolster the U.S. domestic supply chain and reduce reliance on Chinese imports. This strategy is intended to spur the growth of the American rare earth magnet manufacturing industry. Concrete examples of this domestic expansion include E-Vac building a sintered NdFeB magnet plant in Sumter, South Carolina, and MP Materials constructing a similar facility in Texas, with both companies securing long-term supply agreements with automaker GM. <4> Market analysts anticipated an improvement in the overall market sentiment for rare earths in the fourth quarter of 2024, largely driven by expected seasonal increases in downstream demand for magnets, specifically Pr-Nd alloy. Projections from Galaxy Securities supported this outlook, forecasting that global demand growth for Pr-Nd oxide (9%) would outpace supply growth (5-6%), thereby improving the supply-demand balance. While China Rare Earth confirmed that prices for major rare earth products did partially rebound in Q4 after fluctuating at low levels in Q2 and Q3, other analyses indicated that the actual downstream market demand ultimately fell short of initial expectations. <5> Throughout 2024, several major automakers, including General Motors, scaled back their electric vehicle (EV) production targets due to slower-than-expected consumer demand in the U.S. market. A study by J.D. Power in May 2024 identified the lack of charging station availability as a primary reason for consumer apprehension. Specifically, General Motors announced in July 2024 that it was reducing its projected EV output for the year from 300,000 to 250,000 units and delaying the opening of its Orion Assembly EV truck plant until mid-2026. This overarching trend, reported on December 27, 2024, pointed to a potential decrease in the forecasted demand for neodymium magnets from the automotive industry. <6> The American Clean Power Association (ACP) and Wood Mackenzie Power & Renewables jointly released the 'US Wind Energy Monitor | Q4 2024' report on December 17, 2024. This recurring report provides data-driven insights and expert analysis on the U.S. onshore and offshore wind markets. The comprehensive analysis covers policy changes, the impacts of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), project timelines, and supply chain strategies, making it a key resource for developers, investors, utilities, and policymakers to understand market trends. <7> Market analysis reports project significant growth for the global industrial robotics market, driven by widespread automation in manufacturing and other sectors, with one projection anticipating a market valuation of over $55 billion in 2025. This expansion is significant for neodymium, a crucial element in the high-performance magnets used in industrial robot motors and grippers. A late 2024 analysis indicated that while the long-term trend is positive, the market faced challenges, with global robot shipments projected to decline slightly. This was partly due to weaker-than-expected sales to the automotive industry in the U.S. and Europe during the latter half of 2024. However, a gradual recovery is anticipated in 2025, supported by expected increases in machinery investments and a broader rebound in the global manufacturing sector. Forecasts suggest that by 2026, the growth rate for industrial robot shipments will return to over 7%. <8> China's Northern Rare Earth Group announced on August 1, 2024, that its listed prices for rare earth products for that month would be unchanged from July 2024. The price for praseodymium-neodymium oxide was held at 384,800 yuan per ton. This decision by a major global supplier had a significant impact on market confidence at the beginning of the month. While prices were stable at the time of the announcement, by the end of August, praseodymium-neodymium oxide prices had increased by 7.5% compared to the beginning of the month. <9> On July 16, 2024, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced nearly $10 million in funding for two projects aimed at lowering the costs and reducing the environmental impact of producing rare earth elements and other critical minerals from coal and its by-products. The projects, awarded under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, will concentrate on advanced laboratory and bench-scale testing to improve the economic viability of separation and refining technologies. <10> China has implemented significant new controls over its rare earth industry through two distinct key actions. Firstly, on December 21, 2023, the government officially banned the export of technology for extracting and separating rare earths. [7, 12, 11] This was followed by the announcement on June 29, 2024, of a broader set of regulations titled the 'Regulations on the Administration of Rare Earths', which became effective on October 1, 2024. [2, 5] These comprehensive regulations, signed by Premier Li Qiang, establish stricter state control over the entire rare earth supply chain, including mining, smelting, and trading. [3, 4] Key measures include the implementation of a total quantity control system for mining and separation, and the establishment of a product traceability system. [3, 5] Given that China processes nearly 90% of the world's rare earths, these actions are anticipated to have a substantial impact on the global supply chain and have heightened concerns in countries like the United States, which rely heavily on Chinese rare earth imports. [7, 11]

The projects, awarded under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, will concentrate on advanced laboratory and bench-scale testing to improve the economic viability of separation and refining technologies.

Specifically, General Motors announced in July 2024 that it was reducing its projected EV output for the year from 300,000 to 250,000 units and delaying the opening of its Orion Assembly EV truck plant until mid-2026. The supply disruption coincided with a period of peak seasonal demand from key sectors like electric vehicles and wind turbines, creating a significant supply gap for Chinese manufacturers. <2> In July 2025, the price of Neodymium Oxide saw a significant surge of 16.36%, reaching $73,418.65 per metric ton. This price increase was part of a broader trend of rising rare earth prices, driven by a combination of tight supply and robust demand, particularly from the electric vehicle and wind turbine sectors. The surge was influenced by several market factors, including China's export restrictions and a halt in raw material exports from U.S. producer MP Materials to China, which created a significant supply gap. In China, the benchmark price for NdPr alloy jumped from approximately ¥545,000 per metric ton at the start of July to ¥635,000 by July 28. This statement came in light of recent U.S.-China trade negotiations and China's dominance in the production and refining of these critical materials. SEIA clarified that while rare earth elements are not directly used in solar panels, they are essential components of inverters, which convert electricity from DC to AC. Specifically, the association noted the use of yttrium, lanthanum, and cerium oxide in ceramic capacitors, and neodymium in magnets for internal sensors and fans within these inverters. The organization highlighted the nation's heavy dependence on China for these materials, noting that even the one active commercial-scale rare earth mine in the U.S. sends some of its output to China for final processing. <4> General Motors (GM) has entered into a multi-year supply agreement with Noveon Magnetics, the only operational U.S. manufacturer of sintered neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) rare earth magnets. Under the deal, announced on August 6, 2025, Noveon will supply American-made magnets for use in components for GM's full-size SUVs and trucks. Deliveries of the magnets began in July 2025. [6, 10, 13] Furthermore, the partnership includes a $150 million DoD loan to expand heavy rare earth separation capabilities at MP Materials' Mountain Pass facility and supports the development of a second magnet manufacturing plant, the "10X Facility," backed by $1 billion in financing from JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs. [6, 13, 14] As a direct consequence of the agreement, MP Materials has ceased shipping rare earth materials to China. [4, 9] <8> Market analysts on July 2, 2025, forecasted a complex pricing landscape for neodymium in 2025, with a projected price range between $80 to $120 per kilogram, citing the volatile nature of rare earth markets. In mid-July, the U.S. Department of Defense established a guaranteed minimum price of $110 per kilogram for NdPr oxide from domestic producer MP Materials to incentivize production outside of China. [17] Subsequently, by late August, prices in China surged by 40% since July to approximately $88/kg following a halt in raw material exports from MP Materials to China. [6] As of early September 2025, reported market prices show divergence, with some retail-focused sources listing prices as high as $137.80 per kg, while benchmark commodity trackers indicate prices around $107.55/kg. [4, 12, 16] This price volatility is underpinned by strong and growing demand from the electric vehicle and renewable energy sectors, compounded by geopolitical tensions and strategic supply chain shifts involving the US and China. [3, 8, 9] <9> Projections for the third and fourth quarters of 2024 suggested a potential stabilization in neodymium prices, with multiple commodity research firms anticipating moderate growth. This outlook was largely driven by expanding demand from the green technology sector, particularly for use in electric vehicles and wind turbines. [1] While one source indicated these preliminary projections foresaw moderate growth [1], other analyses from mid-2024 pointed to a surplus of neodymium for the remainder of the year, with market tightness and potential price increases not expected until 2026. [5, 6] Another viewpoint suggested that a market improvement and increased purchasing activity could occur in the fourth quarter of 2024. [5, 6] Forecasts from Argus Media also indicated a future imbalance between supply and demand beginning in 2025, which is expected to lead to price increases. [7]

(USAR) has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Less Common Metals (LCM), a UK-based producer of rare earth metals and alloys. Specifically, the association noted the use of yttrium, lanthanum, and cerium oxide in ceramic capacitors, and neodymium in magnets for internal sensors and fans within these inverters. Under the deal, announced on August 6, 2025, Noveon will supply American-made magnets for use in components for GM's full-size SUVs and trucks. Deliveries of the magnets began in July 2025. This strategic partnership is aimed at building a more resilient domestic supply chain for critical automotive materials and reducing reliance on imported rare earth minerals.
